newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: COCA-COLA GIVES S.AFRICA VOTE OF CONFIDENCE.
newsitem.headline: COCA-COLA GIVES S.AFRICA VOTE OF CONFIDENCE.

text.p: U.S. soft drinks giant Coca-Cola Co has given South Africa a major vote of confidence by pledging an investment of more than one billion rand over the next five years, analysts said on Monday.
"It's a token of confidence towards South Africa and shows the potential growth for consumer spending in this country," said Mike Brown, chief economist at Societe Generale Frankel Pollak.
Coca-Cola president Doug Ivester said the spending by Coke and its seven South African bottlers was designed to double sales over the next five to seven years.
Brown said the move by a major U.S. company was particularly encouraging in the light of last month's diplomatic spat between Pretoria and Washington over possible South African arms sales to Syria.
"It's interesting that an American investment should take place at this time when some people are expressing concerns about U.S.-South African relations," he said.

News of the billion-rand deal helped push the rand through 4.53 against the dollar to its best level in 3-1/2 months on Monday as foreign exchange dealers cheered another positive sign in the current bull market.
Dealers said the Coca-Cola deal was particularly welcome given its long-term nature.

Although South Africa -- back as a firm favourite among emerging markets this year -- saw significant inflows in January, most has been volatile portfolio cash which can flow out as fast as it came in.
Corporate financiers say there are signs of renewed interest from companies around the world looking to make direct fixed investments in South Africa.

"There hasn't been a flood from anywhere -- we're seeing fairly constant across-the-board interest," David Perlstein, head partner or corporate finance at Ernst & Young in Johannesburg, told Reuters last week.
Talk is rife that General Motors Corp may be about to return following an 11 year absence after Delta Motor Corp said it was discussing closer links with the car giant.
Two Japanese concerns, Komatsu Ltd and Itochu Corp, said last week they were investing 90 million rand in a construction equipment joint venture with Anglo American Industrial Corp Ltd .
And Japan's Nissan Motor confirmed that it could take a stake running into hundreds of millions of rand in South Africa's Automakers Ltd .
Direct inward foreign investment into South Africa jumped from 820 million rands in 1994 to 3.7 billion rand in 1995, following the first all-race elections in April 1994.

Last year the figure is likely to have topped 4.0 billion rand, according to Trade and Industry Minister Alec Erwin, who said in an interview last week that investment had increased some seven to eight percent in 1996.
